I think the main problem with solar is that it is intermittent - no power at night, no power when it is cloudy. So then you need some sort of energy storage system, which significantly adds to the cost. And batteries aren't so great at long term storage. Depending on how everything is made, there's even a question as to whether the solar panels + battery storage system will generate more energy that it takes to manufacture and install. Efficiency is important, but ensuring that the systems make an "energy profit" is even more important.

There for energy profit is Energy Return on Energy Invested, or EROEI. Most studies agree that solar has a high EROEI. Note that batteries also aren't the only energy storage system- a number of countries used pumped storage where you pump a lot of water high up and then recover it using hydroelectric power. See summary here. This generally works better than batteries but has other disadvantages (chief among them the need for favorable geology). However, wind power works even better as a complement to solar power since while it is also intermittent, wind is often highest when solar power is not available. Wind is generally stronger during night time and during stormy weather which is exactly when you get very little solar power.

I used the phrase "most" for a reason. What you are doing is taking the most pessimistic set of estimates for solar with pumped hydro which is a specific setting. Among other issues, it essentially assumes that one is putting pumped hydro pretty much everywhere, not just where it is a cheap technology. In practice, that's obviously not going to happen. Note that as long as EROEI > 1 (or equivalently log EOREI >0) then that's ok. (I'm going to resist going on my usual rant about how log EROEI is a more natural measure for efficiency of energy sources when one is talking about systems with storage or systems only a bit above breakeven.)

And again, the key here isn't to store wind or solar by and large (except as necessary) but rather to use both and take advantage that most of the time when one is not active the other one is.

But you are essentially correct in that a grid cannot rely on 100% solar or even anywhere near that without substantial improvements in technology which don't at present seem to be happening. (And most of the repeated battery improvement claims and claimed improvements in solar really are hype). A combination of wind, solar with some support from others such as nuclear and hydroelectric has more of a chance. Unfortunately, at least some dependence on fossil fuels is going to have to continue to the indefinite future due to the severe limitations of alternative energies at this point. That's the EROEI necessary for crude oil to work. This is a common misunderstanding that that's general necessary EROEI.
